copyright: Building detail of Registan Square, Samarkand, Uzbekistan (© Piero M. Bianchi/Getty Images)
description: Stand in Registan Square and it's easy to see why it is considered the architectural heart of Samarkand—one of Central Asia's oldest cities. This plaza in Uzbekistan is framed by three magnificent madrasas—Islamic centres of learning—whose soaring portals draw the eye upwards. Yet some of the square's greatest treasures reveal themselves only when you look closer.

copyright: Whale shark and golden trevally, Cenderawasih Bay, West Papua, Indonesia (© Pete Oxford/Nature Picture Library)
description: Today, International Whale Shark Day makes room for the world's largest fish. Despite their name, whale sharks are not whales but fish, reaching lengths of up to 18 metres and weighing around 18 tonnes. Found in warm tropical seas, they glide through the water with their mouths open, filtering plankton, fish eggs and other tiny prey. This species' distinctive white-spot patterns are unique to each individual, much like human fingerprints.

copyright: Notting Hill Carnival, London (© Sebastian Remme/Alamy Live News)
description: Some weekends ask you to slow down. This one turns the volume up. Streets become dance floors, steel pans replace traffic noise, and the scent of Caribbean food follows every step. At Notting Hill Carnival, London's roads don't just close to traffic, they open to celebration.

copyright: Mont-Saint-Michel during high tide, Manche, Normandy, France (© Clement LEONARD/Getty Images)
description: At sunset, Mont-Saint‑Michel rises from the waters of Normandy, France, like a fortress shaped by the sea. Perched on a rocky tidal island, the abbey and village stand at the centre of one of Europe's most dramatic coastal settings. Twice a day, the sea retreats to reveal vast stretches of sand before surging back to reclaim the landscape. At high tide, the mount becomes an island once again. For centuries, travellers timed their journeys to this rhythm, crossing the flats when conditions allowed and watching the sea return hours later.

copyright: Lesser flamingo flock, Lake Magadi, Kenya (© Denis-Huot/Nature Picture Library)
description: Imagine a world without the natural wonders that hold about 90% of Earth's surface freshwater. Lakes are among our planet's most valuable resources, providing clean water, supporting wildlife, regulating climate and sustaining communities worldwide. Recognising their importance, the United Nations designated 27 August as World Lake Day, first observed in 2025. Earth is home to more than 117 million lakes covering nearly 4% of its land surface. Together, they sustain countless ecosystems, while Lake Baikal in Russia alone holds about one-fifth of the world's surface liquid freshwater. Yet many lakes face growing pressure from pollution, overuse and climate change.

copyright: Auroras over Kirkjufell, Iceland (© Cavan Images/Alamy)
description: As darker nights return to Iceland, visitors will soon look to the skies for a chance to see the aurora borealis. Better known as the northern lights, this luminous phenomenon occurs when charged particles from the sun collide with oxygen and nitrogen high in Earth's atmosphere, creating shimmering ribbons of green, pink, purple and sometimes red light. From September to April, Iceland's northern location and long winter nights make it one of the world's finest places to witness the display.

copyright: Aerial view of surfers, Santa Catarina, Brazil (© Wonderful Nature/Shutterstock)
description: Off the coast of Santa Catarina in southern Brazil, the image captures a familiar ritual: surfers waiting beyond the breaking waves, their boards rising and falling with the Atlantic. From above, almost nothing seems to happen. But that's when the real work begins.
